title: Why Struggle Still Matters in a Digital Age
author: Jonathan Boymal
summary: Jonathan Boymal argues that effortful, error-prone learning is the mechanism of learning and not a sign of failure, and that generative AI tempts students to skip it. He draws on research on error-related brain responses, psychological safety, productive failure and desirable difficulties to show that harder practice often produces better long-term retention and transfer. He sorts mistakes into stretch, aha-moment, sloppy and high-stakes types, each calling for a different response. Citing Oakley and colleagues, he defends memorization and schema-building against cognitive offloading. He ends by describing human learning as embodied, emotional and slow, something AI cannot replicate. Boymal's one archived piece sits in Classical Education, but this article's argument is learning science, so it goes under Learning & Curriculum.
points: Students who expect learning to be quick and certain read effort as failure, when effort is often the sign of progress.
Errors trigger neural adaptation, and a classroom where mistakes are welcomed encourages risk-taking and persistence.
Productive failure and desirable difficulties such as spacing, interleaving and self-testing feel worse in the moment but win on long-term retention and transfer.
Sorting mistakes into stretch, aha, sloppy and high-stakes types helps teachers choose the right response to each.
Offloading knowledge to AI undermines the schemas that fluent thinking depends on, so memory and effort still matter.
quotes: Research suggests that many students believe learning should be fixed, simple, certain, and quick. When learning feels effortful, they may misinterpret that struggle as a sign of failure, not progress.

What’s remarkable is that even without conscious attention, errors can prompt the brain to adapt. Mistakes, in other words, are catalysts for neuroplasticity. They prime the brain to rewire, especially during sleep, helping us grow.

One way to harness the power of error is through “productive failure.” For example, instead of starting with instruction, this method can begin with problem-solving, even if students haven’t yet fully learned the concepts. Struggling upfront fosters deeper understanding later.

The same holds true for what cognitive scientists call “desirable difficulties.” Spacing out practice, switching between tasks, or self-testing while studying all make learning harder in the moment but better in the long run. These techniques pose a paradox: they feel like they’re not working. Performance dips in the short term. But when it’s time to apply knowledge, learners who embraced difficulty outperform those who played it safe.

A recent chapter by Barbara Oakley and colleagues pushes back against the idea that memorisation is obsolete in the digital age. Relying too heavily on “cognitive offloading” can undermine our ability to think fluently, spot errors, or apply knowledge creatively.

Generative AI gives the impression that knowledge is now instant. With the right prompt, we can summon answers, generate summaries, or solve complex problems. But this convenience creates an illusion: that mastery can be downloaded.

In the end, human learning is embodied, emotional, social, and deeply contextual. Our minds are shaped by our bodies, our histories, our relationships, and the environments we move through. Emotions like curiosity and belonging ignite learning. Culture and lived experience shape how we think, what we value, and how we grow.
